question: What is the average number of pairs of consecutive integers in a randomly selected subset of \(5\) distinct integers chosen from the set \(\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 30\}?\) (For example the set \(\{1, 17, 18, 19, 30\}\) has \(2\) pairs of consecutive integers.)
solution:
The total number of consecutive pairs across all subsets can be counted one fixed pair at a time, then divided by the number of subsets.

There are \(\binom{30}{5}\) equally likely subsets. Give each subset one mark for every consecutive pair it contains. Overlapping pairs receive separate marks, as required by the question.

There are \(29\) possible consecutive pairs, from \(\{1,2\}\) through \(\{29,30\}\). For any fixed pair, a subset containing it is completed by choosing three of the other \(28\) integers. Thus that pair contributes \(\binom{28}{3}\) marks, and the total number of marks is
\[
29\binom{28}{3}.
\]
Each subset contributes exactly its own number of consecutive pairs to this total. Therefore the desired average is
\[
\frac{29\binom{28}{3}}{\binom{30}{5}}
=29\cdot\frac{5\cdot4}{30\cdot29}
=\boxed{\frac23},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
A run of \(s\) selected consecutive integers contributes \(s-1\) consecutive pairs. Thus counting subsets by their number of runs gives the full distribution of the pair count.

Represent a subset by \(30\) positions, each marked selected or unselected. A run is a block of selected positions that cannot be extended within the subset. If there are \(r\) runs, their lengths sum to \(5\), so the number of consecutive pairs is \(5-r\).

There are \(\binom{4}{r-1}\) ordered lists of positive run lengths: place \(r-1\) cuts in the four spaces between five selected marks.

The \(25\) unselected marks leave \(26\) gaps, including the two ends. Choose \(r\) of these gaps and insert the runs in order. There are \(\binom{26}{r}\) choices. Different occupied gaps are separated by an unselected mark, so the runs stay distinct. Conversely, every subset uniquely determines its run lengths and occupied gaps. Hence the number of subsets with \(r\) runs is
\[
\binom{4}{r-1}\binom{26}{r}.
\]
This gives all possibilities:

| Runs \(r\) | Consecutive pairs \(5-r\) | Number of subsets |
|---:|---:|---:|
| \(1\) | \(4\) | \(26\) |
| \(2\) | \(3\) | \(1300\) |
| \(3\) | \(2\) | \(15600\) |
| \(4\) | \(1\) | \(59800\) |
| \(5\) | \(0\) | \(65780\) |

For example, the \(r=3\) entry is \(\binom42\binom{26}{3}=6\cdot2600=15600\). Using these counts as weights, the average is
\[
\frac{4(26)+3(1300)+2(15600)+59800}{\binom{30}{5}}
=\frac{95004}{142506}
=\boxed{\frac23},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Count consecutive runs
